title: Rydberg Equation — Derivation from Bohr's Model and Numericals
notes: How the Rydberg equation follows from Bohr's theory, what the Rydberg constant means, and the standard numerical patterns built on it.

R is the wave number of the hydrogen series limit (n₁ = 1, n₂ → ∞): $\bar{\nu}_{limit}=R$, λ = 91.2 nm. Because m appears in R, the constant is slightly isotope-dependent (reduced-mass correction): R(²H) ≈ R(¹H) × 1.00027 — the basis of measuring deuterium in heavy water spectroscopically.
• Wavelength of a given line: pick n₁ (series) and n₂ (upper level); compute $\bar{\nu}$, invert for λ.
• First line of a series: n₂ = n₁ + 1.
• Identification: given λ and a series, solve for n₂; given two lines, form their difference to get a third line (Ritz combination principle).
• Hydrogen-like ions: multiply by Z² (He⁺ Balmer lines are 4× the wave number of hydrogen's).
R is quoted both as 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ and 109 677 cm⁻¹. Convert before mixing: 1 cm⁻¹ = 100 m⁻¹; λ(nm) = 10⁷/ν̄(cm⁻¹).
confusion: ❌ R is an empirical fitted constant with no origin. ✅ Bohr derived it from m, e, h and c — a theoretical prediction confirmed by experiment.
❌ ν̄ is the frequency. ✅ It is the wave number (1/λ); frequency ν = c·ν̄.
❌ The same R applies unchanged to He⁺. ✅ Multiply by Z² (and apply the reduced-mass correction for precision).

universalFacts: R was known experimentally to 6 figures before Bohr — the theory matched without fitting.
The reduced-mass shift of the D line (²H) versus H line identified deuterium in 1932.
Ritz's combination principle: the wave number of one line equals the sum/difference of two others sharing a level.
examples: **Problem:** Wave number of the Paschen limit. **Solution:** ν̄ = R/9 = 1.22×10⁶ m⁻¹ → λ = 820.4 nm.
importantNotes: Keep R in one unit system throughout a calculation; the cm⁻¹↔m⁻¹ factor of 100 is the classic slip.
For He⁺, Li²⁺ multiply by Z² before inverting for λ.

summary: The Rydberg equation falls straight out of Bohr's theory. A photon emitted in a jump n₂ → n₁ carries hν = E₂ − E₁ = 2π²me⁴Z²/h² · (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²); dividing by hc gives the wave number ν̄ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with R = 2π²me⁴/h³c = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ = 109 677 cm⁻¹, so an empirical formula known to six figures before 1913 emerged from theory. R is also the wave number of the Lyman series limit (λ = 91.2 nm), and because m appears in it the constant is slightly isotope-dependent — the reduced-mass correction that let Urey identify deuterium in 1932. The standard numerical patterns are the wavelength of a given line, the series limit from ν̄ = RZ²/n₁², the first line with n₂ = n₁ + 1, and identification of an unknown n₂; for hydrogen-like ions every wave number is multiplied by Z².
importantConcepts: Derivation: hν = E₂ − E₁ = 2π²me⁴Z²/h² · (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) leads to ν̄ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
R = 2π²me⁴/h³c = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ = 109 677 cm⁻¹, derived by Bohr and confirmed to six figures
R is the wave number of the Lyman limit (n₁ = 1, n₂ → ∞), corresponding to λ = 91.2 nm
Reduced-mass correction: R(²H) ≈ R(¹H) × 1.00027, the basis of detecting deuterium spectroscopically
Numerical patterns: line wavelength, series limit, first line of a series, unknown n₂, and the Z² factor for hydrogen-like ions
importantStatements: ν̄ is the wave number 1/λ, not the frequency; frequency is ν = c·ν̄.
R was not fitted: Bohr derived it from m, e, h and c, and theory matched experiment without adjustment.
For He⁺ and Li²⁺ the wave number is multiplied by Z², so the wavelengths are 1/Z² of hydrogen's.
R must be used in one unit system throughout: 1 cm⁻¹ = 100 m⁻¹ and λ(nm) = 10⁷/ν̄(cm⁻¹).
Ritz's combination principle: one line's wave number equals the sum or difference of two others sharing a level.

keyPoints: ν̄ = RZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²) with n₂ > n₁ is the whole formula.
Series limit: set n₂ → ∞ to get ν̄ = RZ²/n₁².
First line of a series: n₂ = n₁ + 1.
λ(nm) = 1240/ΔE(eV) and λ(nm) = 10⁷/ν̄(cm⁻¹) are the two conversion workhorses.
specialNotes: Convert cm⁻¹ to m⁻¹ by multiplying by 100; mixing the two is the commonest error in this topic.
The Balmer formula was empirical until Bohr derived it — the derivation was the model's greatest success.
The reduced-mass shift of the D lines was small (0.027%) yet large enough to detect deuterium.
examShortTricks: Keep R in one unit system for the whole calculation.
For He⁺, Li²⁺ multiply by Z² before inverting for λ.
If a question gives λ and asks for n₂, substitute and solve the 1/n₂² term directly.
